citation: docs/architecture.md, one action path: every surface sends the same Request, so a CLI is a way of spelling one rather than a second set of behaviours. The words a command line uses are Muster's own policy and there is no oracle above them; what each field means is documented on the messages themselves in proto/muster.proto. kan a_26BJb2n6o and a_294MvlG1E.
why: What `muster pane new --down --run claude` becomes is the whole contract between an agent and the window it is sitting in, and it is the part that outlives this implementation - a `muster` rewritten in anything else has to turn the same words into the same requests. Three shapes of outcome are pinned: the request a line becomes, the refusal a line earns from us, and the *kind* of complaint clap makes about a line it cannot read. The kind rather than the wording, because the wording is clap's and would change under a version bump, while `an unknown flag is refused rather than swallowed` is the promise. Fields left at their protobuf default are absent here, so a case reads as what somebody actually said: `side` and a rename's `name` are the exceptions, the first because every split has a side and the default is the point, and the second because an empty name is what takes a name away.

cases.name: asking what daemons are on this machine names no window and no pane
cases.why:
The one verb here that is about the machine rather than about a window. `muster window` answers what this window is attached to; this answers what is on the machine at all, including the daemons no window is attached to - which are the ones that accumulate.

It takes nothing, and that is the case. A pane ref would be meaningless and a daemon ref would be asking about the thing being enumerated. A verb that took a filter would be a verb somebody could use to narrow a census down to the row they already expected.

cases.name: the whole window is one read
cases.why: An agent has no eyes, so this is half the value of the surface. One request rather than a question per pane, because a caller that has to ask again for each cannot see them at one moment.

cases.name: a split with no side lands to the right
cases.why: Right is where cmd+d puts one, and the CLI and the keyboard have to agree about what `a split` means - a default that matched no chord would make the same word mean two things depending on which surface you used.

cases.name: a pane made from inside a pane splits the one it is running in
cases.why: The mechanism the whole scenario rests on: an agent told to split two panes below itself names no pane, and MUSTER_PANE is the only thing that can say which one it is. Muster puts it in the environment of the very request that creates the pane.

cases.name: a named pane beats the one this is running in
cases.why: An agent arranging panes for others addresses them by name while sitting in its own, so the flag has to win. If the environment won, an integrator could only ever act on itself.

cases.name: an exported but empty MUSTER_PANE is not an answer
cases.why: An exported-but-empty variable is a normal state of a shell profile, and of a herdr pane restored after a daemon restart - those get no launch environment at all. Read as a real answer it would send a request naming the pane called `""`, which no window holds, instead of falling through to the pane the keyboard is on.

cases.name: a pane made for an agent carries its program and its name
cases.why: The gesture the cards are about, in one line. Both travel with the split rather than as requests afterwards: the program because a caller sending it itself would race the new shell's first prompt, and the name because a rename arriving later leaves the pane briefly nameless in every window showing it.

cases.name: a pane can be asked for on a machine rather than beside a pane
cases.why: The only way to reach a machine you have no pane on, which is every devenv on the day it is attached and any machine whose last pane you closed. Every other route to a new pane goes through an existing one - a split inherits its pane's machine, a tab takes the workspace from a pane - so without this a machine that reaches zero panes is one nothing in Muster can put a pane back on. The side still travels, because a machine already showing panes splits the one its region has the keyboard on.

cases.name: a machine named from inside a pane does not carry that pane
cases.why: The case that would silently do the opposite of what was asked. $MUSTER_PANE is sent whenever nobody names a pane, and the window reads a named pane as the whole address - so a `--daemon` that let the environment through would send the request straight back to the machine it was trying to leave, and would look like it worked. A pane typed beside --daemon is a different request, which puts the new pane in that pane's tab; the pane nobody typed is never one.

cases.name: the keyboard moves only when asked
cases.why: take_focus is absent from every other case here, and that is the point: an agent opening three panes would otherwise drag somebody's cursor through all three. Pressing a key means `I made this and I am looking at it`; a script means `make it and leave my cursor alone`.

cases.name: an empty --run is nothing to run
cases.why: A script interpolating a variable that turned out empty would otherwise ask the window to wait for a prompt and then type nothing, which costs the readiness wait and leaves a pane looking like it failed at something.

cases.name: text that asks for a return is submitted
cases.why: The other half of an agent instructing another. Return is a flag rather than a newline in the text because the two differ once a program is reading: Return is encoded against the pane's live modes, and a bare newline inside a bracketed paste is text rather than a submission.

cases.name: asking to be sure the text arrived is a third thing the send carries
cases.why:
Not a second command, and that is the point of it being a flag. A caller that sent and then read the pane itself would be two requests with a gap between them, and the gap is where a harness redraws - so the check has to be part of the send and the window has to make it.

It is independent of `--enter`, because the two answer different questions. `--enter` asks for a Return; this asks whether the message can be seen on the pane afterwards. A caller that wants a message left sitting on a prompt still wants to know it got there.

cases.name: text with no return waits on the prompt
cases.why: The difference between telling an agent something and leaving a line sitting there for a person to look at. Both are wanted, so the flag has to be the only thing that decides.

cases.name: unquoted text arrives in pieces and is sent as one line
cases.why: Somebody typing an instruction will forget the quotes, and joining is what they meant - the alternative is a refusal for a command line with exactly one possible reading. Single spaces, because the shell already ate whatever else was between the words.

cases.name: a double dash makes text of something that looks like a flag
cases.why: Instructions to an agent contain flags. Without this there would be no way to send the characters `--enter` to a pane, and the failure would be silent: the flag would be honoured and the text would go out one word shorter than it was written.

cases.name: a brief can come from a file, resolved against where the command was typed
cases.why: Text with quotes in it has to survive every shell between the caller and this command, and a file crosses none of them (kan a_2M9T8iOgk). A relative path means what it means everywhere else, the directory `muster` was run in, and it is resolved here rather than by the read so a case can pin it.

cases.name: a lone hyphen reads the text from stdin
cases.why: The other half of the card: a caller holding the text in a pipe or a heredoc. Under `laptop run` the command itself travels over stdin, so this cannot be the only way in, and `--file` is the one that works there.

given.input: it's a brief with 'quotes' in it

send_to_pane.text: it's a brief with 'quotes' in it

cases.name: trailing newlines are dropped the way command substitution drops them
cases.why: A file ends in a newline by convention, not because anybody meant one to reach the pane - and `--enter` is how a caller asks for Return. Dropping every trailing newline, as `"$(cat PATH)"` does, means `--file` sends exactly what callers were sending by hand before it existed. Newlines inside the text stay: a multi-line brief arrives as one paste.

cases.name: a hyphen inside the text is text
cases.why: Only a hyphen standing alone means stdin. One among other words is part of a sentence, and reading stdin there would hang a command that had its whole text already.

cases.name: a file and text on the command line together is refused
cases.why: Two sources for one message, and no reading of which the caller meant. Joining them would type something nobody wrote.

cases.name: a send with neither text nor a file is refused
cases.why: There is nothing to type. An empty string is still text and still allowed, because `pane send "" --enter` is how a caller presses Return on its own.

cases.name: a quoted tilde in a file path is refused rather than guessed at
cases.why: The shell expands a tilde and this command does not, so one that arrives here arrived quoted. Joined onto the working directory it names a file nobody has, and the refusal is more use than a read error about `/work/~/brief.md`.

expect.refused: `--file ~/brief.md` still has its tilde, so the shell did not expand it - quoting is what usually does that, and muster does not expand one itself. Nothing was sent. Write the path out, or leave it unquoted so the shell expands it first.

cases.name: the layout is the same read, asking for the arrangement and the sizes too
cases.why: Where every tab's panes sit and how big each is, for a person reading the terminal and an agent reading JSON. A flag on the one read rather than a verb, so it composes with --json, --socket and the answer for every window; and asked for rather than always answered, because the sizes are a question to every daemon where the ordinary read asks none.

cases.name: a layout watched is a watch that says when the layout may have moved, and the layout read again
cases.why: A drawing per change makes the layout a live view. The window cannot say when a drawing changed, only when it may have, so the watch asks to hear that and the CLI reads the layout again to find out; a pane's state changing is not the layout changing, and draws nothing.

cases.name: watching a window is one request that asks for everything
cases.why: The shape an integrator waiting on several agents wants: one connection, and a line each time any of them changes (kan a_2M9T8O6dL). It names no pane and no state, which is what the window reads as every pane, for good.

cases.name: watching is about the one window, not the windows in the plural
cases.why: `window list`, `new` and `reopen` are about windows in the plural, and a watch holds one connection to one window. Both at once has no reading.

cases.name: a wait names the panes, the states that end it, and how long to hold out
cases.why: Several panes because an integrator waits on the first of its workers to finish, and a comma list because `idle,blocked` - finished, or stuck on a question - is the usual pair. The timeout is the caller's patience, not something the window is told, so it stays out of the request.

cases.name: a wait can end when an agent settles into waiting on its own work
cases.why: `waiting` is a word `muster window` prints, for an idle agent that said it ended its turn to wait on work it started. It is not `idle`, which is an agent with nothing left to do, so a caller who wants either names both.

cases.name: a wait does not wait on the pane it is running in
cases.why: Every other pane command falls back to $MUSTER_PANE. This one cannot mean it: the pane the command is running in is busy running the command, so a wait on it has no useful answer, and a caller who left `--pane` off meant some other pane.

cases.name: a state nobody is ever in is refused by the command line
cases.why: A typo in a state would otherwise wait for something that never happens, which from outside is indistinguishable from an agent still working. The six words are the ones `muster window` prints.

cases.name: a wait on context alone needs no state
cases.why: An orchestrator compacting a worker before it runs out wants to hear when its context fills, whatever it is doing then. The percent travels as a float because that is how an agent reports it.

cases.name: a wait on context and a state ends on whichever comes first
cases.why: A worker that finishes before its context fills has also given the orchestrator its moment, so the two are one wait rather than two in parallel.

cases.name: a context no agent can be at is refused by the command line
cases.why: Context is said in percent. Zero is met by every agent that has said anything, and more than 100 by none, so either is a wait that means nothing.

cases.name: a wait on nothing is refused by the command line
cases.why: With neither a state nor a context there is nothing that could end it, and `window --watch` is the command for hearing everything.

cases.name: a wait that gives up at once is refused
cases.why: Zero seconds would be answered before the window could say anything, so it reads as a pane that never got there. Somebody asking whether a pane is already somewhere asks with a second.

cases.name: compacting a pane's agent says what to keep
cases.why: An orchestrator compacting a worker names it and says what the summary must not lose. The focus arrives in pieces from a shell and is one line by the time it is typed.

cases.name: an agent compacts itself by naming nothing
cases.why: An agent asking to be compacted is running in the pane it means, as for every pane command, and a compaction needs nothing to keep.

cases.name: renaming a pane says what to call it
cases.why: A person running fifteen agents wants to say which is which in their own words, and this is the surface a script sets those names from.

cases.name: an empty name takes the name away
cases.why: One spelling for `no name` rather than two, and the only way to undo a rename. Absence and the empty string have to stay distinguishable here, which is why this field is written out even when it is empty.

cases.name: closing with nothing named closes the pane this is running in
cases.why: Consistent with every other command, and worth pinning precisely because it is the surprising one: an agent that runs this ends the shell its own process is in. The help says so; this makes sure the behaviour matches what the help says.

cases.name: reattaching a pane names the pane and nothing else
cases.why: The way back from a pane the window has stopped drawing while its agent is still running. Every other way back ends the agent - `pane close` by design, quitting the app for every pane at once - so this asks for the one thing a dark pane needs, and the request carries nothing but which pane, because there is nothing else to say about it.

cases.name: reattaching with nothing named reattaches the pane this is running in
cases.why: The same fallback every pane verb has, and the one that matters most here: an agent watching its own pane go dark cannot name it from inside, and a person typing this is usually already in the window it is about.

cases.name: focus with nothing named goes to the pane this is running in
cases.why: An agent asking to be looked at, which is the one thing in this vocabulary that reaches for a person's attention rather than for a pane.

cases.name: focus with nothing to focus is refused rather than sent
cases.why: The one command where an empty pane is not an answer: everywhere else the window reads it as `the pane the keyboard is on`, and asking to focus the focused pane is not something to ask for. Refused here rather than at the window, because only out here is it known that the reason is a missing MUSTER_PANE - the window would only be able to say that no pane was named.

expect.refused: `muster focus` needs a pane, a direction or a place, and $MUSTER_PANE is not set - so this is not running inside a pane Muster made. Name one: `muster focus p1w3r07bsd`, or say `--next`. `muster window` lists them.

cases.name: zoom with nothing named means the pane the keyboard is on
cases.why: Run from a terminal outside Muster there is no MUSTER_PANE, and the useful answer is still `the pane somebody is looking at`. The empty pane id is how every request in the schema spells that, so this sends one rather than refusing.

cases.name: an answer can be asked for as JSON
cases.why: The flag every command takes, and the one an agent always passes. It changes the rendering and never the request, which is what lets the two renderings come from one answer.

cases.name: a window can be named instead of looked for
cases.why: The escape hatch for a caller that is not in a pane and has more than one Muster open, which would otherwise be refused with nothing to do about it.

cases.name: a flag nobody has is refused rather than ignored
cases.why: The commonest mistake an agent makes, and the one that must not pass quietly: a swallowed `--focused` would be a pane that appeared somewhere nobody expected with no sign that anything was wrong.

cases.name: two sides at once is refused
cases.why: A pane lands on one side of another, so there is no honest thing to do with both - and picking one silently would be picking for somebody who has said they are unsure.

cases.name: a pane and a machine put the new pane on that machine, in that pane's tab
cases.why: What right-clicking a pane and picking another machine sends. The machine travels in a field of its own rather than as `daemon_id`, which beside a pane names the machine holding it and is refused when the two disagree - so the window can tell `put it over there` from a caller that got the pane's machine wrong.

cases.name: a verb that does not exist is refused
cases.why: Every word in this vocabulary is one somebody typed from memory. A misspelling has to come back as a refusal naming the verbs there are, rather than as nothing happening.

cases.name: a rename with no name is refused
cases.why: Distinct from the empty name above, which is a deliberate ask. Nothing at all is somebody who has not finished typing, and taking the name away would be the wrong guess at what they meant.

cases.name: a pane name where a window subcommand goes is refused
cases.why: `muster window p1w3r07bsd` reads like a request to describe one pane, and there is no such request. Answering the whole window instead would look like it had been narrowed and had not. Refused as an unknown subcommand rather than a stray argument since `window` grew `list` and `new` under it, which is the more useful of the two complaints: it names what may go there.

cases.name: nothing at all shows what there is
cases.why: A bare `muster` is somebody finding out what this is, so it prints the help rather than complaining about an absence. It still exits non-zero, because nothing was asked and nothing happened.

cases.name: a tab is gone to by name
cases.why: The command the whole card exists for. Before it, a script could read a tab out of `muster window` and had no way to act on it - focusing a pane in the tab was the only route, which means knowing a pane in it. No daemon travels: a tab name is unique across every attached machine, so the window finds which one holds it.

cases.name: going to a tab needs one named
cases.why: Where a pane command falls back to $MUSTER_PANE, this refuses. There is no equivalent for a tab - nothing tells a pane which tab holds it - and `the tab the keyboard is in` is not somewhere to ask to go. Refused by clap rather than here, because a missing positional is exactly what clap is for and its message names the argument.

cases.name: a tab is renamed by name
cases.why: The other half. An agent that made a tab for its own work names it so the person at the keyboard can tell it apart, exactly as it names a pane - and it has to say which tab, because the keyboard is somewhere else.

cases.name: a tab moves into the window this reaches
cases.why: Pulling a tab here is the move a person makes most: it is in another window and they want it in this one. No --window is this window, the one the command reaches, and the tab comes on screen because whoever asked is looking here (kan a_2Mhi0EZlv).

cases.name: a tab moves to a window named by its pid
cases.why: The pid is what `muster window` prints at the head of each window's answer, so a person reads one and types the other. Carried as the words said rather than as a number: a closed window is named, not numbered, and the window decides which it was given.

cases.name: a tab moves to a window that is closed, by name
cases.why: A closed window keeps its tabs and has no process, so its name is the only handle it has. Moving a tab there takes it out of this window now, and it is back when that window is reopened.

cases.name: renaming with no tab means the tab the keyboard is in
cases.why: The empty field, which the schema reads as the tab holding the pane the window's keyboard is on - what the menu item means. Deliberately not the tab this command is running in: nothing in a pane's environment says which tab holds it, and guessing from $MUSTER_PANE would need a second round trip from a parser that is pure by design.

cases.name: an empty name takes a tab's name away
cases.why: The same spelling a pane's rename uses, so one rule covers both: an empty name is the request to go back to being unnamed. How completely that happens is the backend's answer - herdr leaves the tab holding an empty label rather than restoring its number - and the caption then draws the place.

cases.name: a tab is closed by name
cases.why: The verb that was missing: Close Pane existed and emptying a tab one pane at a time was the only route to the same place. A tab name is Muster's own and unique across every machine, so no daemon travels with it.

cases.name: closing with no --tab closes the tab this is running in
cases.why: The fallback going to a tab deliberately does not have. `tab focus` with no tab means nothing - there is no `the one I am already in` to go to - and closing one is exactly that, which is what a menu item means by it.

cases.name: a tab verb that does not exist is refused
cases.why:
`muster tab` has fewer verbs than `muster pane`, and the ones it lacks it lacks for a reason: nothing types into a tab, and nothing reads one. Somebody will try anyway, and a refusal that lists what there is beats a request nobody can build.

This case used to be `tab close`, on the argument that a tab closes when its last pane does. That argument was wrong about what it cost: emptying a tab one pane at a time was the only route to a thing people do, so `tab close` exists now (kan `a_2Ic6mB36E`) and the case moved to a verb that really has no meaning for a tab.

cases.name: a tab is made beside the pane this is running in
cases.why: The other way to make a pane, and until now the one thing a script could not do: splitting was the only route, so anything that did not belong in this tab had nowhere to go. No pane is named, so the tab joins the workspace of the pane this is running in - the same answer cmd+T means by naming nothing.

cases.name: a tab made for an agent carries its program and its name
cases.why: The same intention `pane new --run --name` carries, for the same reason: the program travels with the tab because a caller sending it afterwards would race the new shell's prompt, and the name travels because a rename arriving later leaves the pane briefly nameless. A tab that could be made and not equipped would send every caller back to splitting.

cases.name: a tab made with --focus takes the keyboard
cases.why: The rule `pane new` follows: the keyboard moves only when asked. For a tab that also decides whether it comes on screen, because the tab on screen is where the keyboard is - so without --focus the tab is made behind the one on screen, and an agent opening three tabs does not drag anybody through all three.

cases.name: a tab can be made on a machine rather than beside a pane
cases.why: The same reach as `pane new --daemon`, and on a machine holding nothing the two mean the same thing: a tab lives in a workspace and a machine with no pane has none, so both become the one request that makes a workspace. Spelled on both verbs because a caller reaches for whichever noun they want, and a surface where only one of them could say `over there` would be a rule to remember rather than a rule.

cases.name: a tab is stepped to rather than named
cases.why: The other axis to stepping panes: `focus --next` reaches every pane the window is showing, and this reaches the tabs behind them. A script that has read one tab out of `muster window` can walk the rest without reading again.

cases.name: a tab cannot be both named and stepped to
cases.why: Two answers to one question. Naming a tab and asking for the next one are different intentions, and honouring either silently would be picking for somebody who said both.

cases.name: a tab cannot be asked for both beside a pane and on a machine
cases.why: Unlike `pane new`, where the pane says which tab the new one joins, a new tab joins nothing: the pane would only be saying which machine, and the machine is already said. So naming both is a restatement or a contradiction, and there is no way to tell which from out here.

cases.name: a pane is moved onto another
cases.why: The verb the card is about. The window works out which of the two things this means from where the panes are - the same tab is an exchange, another tab is a move - so one verb here rather than two, and no daemon travels: a pane name is unique across every attached machine.

cases.name: a pane is moved to one side of another
cases.why: What dropping a pane on another pane's edge asks for, from a script. A side is the one thing a move could not say before, and it is what turns a side by side pair into one above the other: the pane goes below the one named, in whichever tab that is, rather than trading places with it.

cases.name: a side is a side of a pane, so it needs --onto
cases.why: A tab has no sides, and a tab of its own has nothing to be beside. Refused while parsing, so a script that meant `--onto X --down` and dropped the pane is told rather than given a pane somewhere else.

cases.name: two sides at once are two answers to one question
cases.why: A pane goes to one side of another. Two is a caller who has not decided, and picking one would put the pane somewhere it was half asked to go.

cases.name: moving with no --pane moves the pane this is running in
cases.why: The rule every pane verb follows, and worth pinning here because moving names two panes and could plausibly have demanded both. An agent asking to be put beside another agent should not have to look up its own name first.

cases.name: moving a pane needs somewhere to put it
cases.why: The half that has no default. Where a pane goes is the whole content of the request, and there is no `the obvious place` for the window to fall back to.

cases.name: a pane is moved into a tab of its own
cases.why: The other destination, and the reason the verb needed one: pulling a pane out of a split used to take `tab new`, this move, and `pane close` to throw away the shell the first command started - three round trips, not atomic, and the keyboard landing in the throwaway on the way past.

cases.name: a tab a move makes can be named
cases.why: `--name` fills the label on the request. The dance this replaces could not set it at all: it made the tab before anything knew what was going into it, so the name would have had to be a fourth command.

cases.name: moving with --new-tab and no --pane moves the pane this is running in
cases.why: The same fallback the rest of the verb has, and it reaches further here: this destination names one pane rather than two, so an agent asking to be pulled out of a split says nothing at all beyond the flag.

cases.name: a move goes to one place or the other, never both
cases.why: Two destinations in one command line is a caller that means two things, and picking one by precedence would carry out a request nobody wrote. Refused where the position flags on other verbs are refused - by the parser, before anything is sent.

cases.name: naming a tab without asking for one is refused
cases.why: `--name` only means anything with `--new-tab`, and a name silently dropped is a tab that comes back unnamed with nothing saying why. Refused against `--onto` rather than made to require `--new-tab`: a bool flag is present in clap's sense whether or not it was typed, so a requirement on one is a requirement nothing can fail, and the required destination group leaves refusing the other half saying exactly the same thing.

cases.name: a relative directory is resolved where the command was run
cases.why: The whole of what a caller means by `../muster-1`, and the one thing nothing on the far side can work out. The window is another process in another directory and the daemon is a third, so a relative path that travels as typed is resolved against a directory nobody chose - which is how three panes meant for sibling worktrees all opened in `$HOME` while every command reported success. Resolved here for the same reason an omitted `--pane` is: this is the only process that knows where the caller is standing.

cases.name: a directory that is already absolute is not touched
cases.why: Where the caller is standing is what a relative path is missing, so a path that is not missing it is not improved by knowing. This also pins that resolution is not silently re-rooting somebody's absolute path against the cwd.

cases.name: the steps in a path are worked out rather than passed on
cases.why: `/src/muster/../muster-1` reaches the same directory and is what a person reads in `muster window` afterwards, so the tidying is worth doing. Lexically, without asking the filesystem: this parser is pure, the answer has to be the same on a machine that has never had these directories, and a path bound for another machine cannot be checked here at all. It is also what a shell's own `cd ..` does, so the two agree about what `..` means.

cases.name: an empty directory is not a directory
cases.why: The empty string is what the schema reads as `the directory the pane being split is in`, which is what a split with no `--cwd` means and what the chord does. So `--cwd ''` has to stay empty rather than become the caller's own directory - resolving it would quietly move every pane made that way.

cases.name: a machine is not somewhere this command can resolve a relative path against
cases.why: `--daemon` is the way to say `over there`, and over there is a machine whose filesystem this command cannot see - very often not even the same operating system. Resolving `../muster-1` against the caller's own directory would send a path that machine has never had, and the daemon would fall back to a home directory exactly as it does today. Refused rather than guessed, because a refusal is the one answer that cannot put a pane somewhere nobody asked for.

expect.refused: `muster pane new --daemon devenv` puts the pane on another machine, and `--cwd ../muster-1` is relative to this one - so there is nothing here to resolve it against. Say where it should start in that machine's own terms: an absolute path. `muster window` lists the panes devenv already holds, and each one's directory is a place a path can be written from.

cases.name: a machine still takes an absolute directory
cases.why: The other half of the refusal above, and the reason it is about the path rather than about `--daemon`: a caller that says where on that machine to start is saying something this command can carry, and carrying it is the only way to open a first pane on a devenv in a particular directory.

cases.name: a tilde the shell did not expand is refused
cases.why: Expanding `~` is the shell's job, so one that arrives here arrives because it was quoted - and joining it to the caller's directory produces `/src/muster/~/x`, a path nobody has. Refused rather than sent, because the daemon's answer to a directory it cannot use is the home directory, which is the silent substitution this whole card is about.

expect.refused: `--cwd ~/src/muster-1` still has its tilde, so the shell did not expand it - quoting is what usually does that. Muster does not expand one either, because `~` is the shell's own spelling of your home directory and a command that guessed at it would be guessing for whoever is on the far side. Write the path out, or leave it unquoted so the shell expands it first.

cases.name: a relative directory with nothing to resolve it against is refused
cases.why: A case with no `cwd` is a command whose own working directory could not be read, which happens when the directory a shell is sitting in has been deleted underneath it. Nothing here can be resolved, and the honest answer is to say so - a path sent unresolved is the bug, and a path resolved against a guess is worse.

expect.refused: `--cwd ../muster-1` is relative and this command cannot tell what directory it is running in, so there is nothing to resolve it against. The usual cause is a shell whose working directory has been deleted or unmounted underneath it. Give an absolute path, or `cd` somewhere that exists and try again.

cases.name: a tab starts where a split does
cases.why: `tab new` takes `--cwd` on the same terms `pane new` does and is the other verb that makes a pane, so a rule that held for one and not the other would be a rule nobody could remember. One helper answers both.

cases.name: a pane is grown by the window's own step
cases.why: What a resize chord means, said from a script. No amount travels, because zero is what the window reads as `your own step` - so a caller with nothing particular in mind gets what the keyboard gets rather than a distance this CLI invented.

cases.name: a divider can be placed exactly
cases.why: The half a chord cannot ask for. A person holds a key down and looks; a script cannot look, so it says how far in one request rather than guessing how many presses that was.

cases.name: resizing needs a direction
cases.why: A resize with no direction is not a smaller request, it is an unfinished one - and unlike a split there is no side that happens anyway to default to.

cases.name: evening a tab out takes no direction and no number
cases.why: The verb the whole card is about. Every other way of moving a divider asks the caller to know where it should end up, and working that out from a tree is exactly what an agent driving a window cannot do by looking - so this says what it wants and lets the window do the arithmetic. No scope travels, because the empty string is what the window reads as `the whole tab`, and the whole tab is what somebody who narrowed nothing means.

cases.name: a scope narrows an equalize to the panes beside this one
cases.why: `row` and `column` are spelled the way somebody looking at the window would spell them rather than the way the tree does, where a row of panes is a `columns` split. The word crosses over once, at the seam, and a command line is not where that should be visible.

cases.name: an equalize takes no fraction
cases.why: Refused rather than ignored. An equalize's shares come out of how many panes hang off each divider, so a caller that also named a fraction meant one of the two - and silently taking the other is how a script ends up believing it asked for something it did not.

cases.name: an equalize is not a direction, and cannot be given with one
cases.why: The five are one question - what should happen to this pane's share - so exactly one of them is an answer. Growing a pane rightwards and evening its tab out are different requests, and a command line asking for both says which one it meant to nobody.

cases.name: a scope beside a direction is refused rather than dropped
cases.why: `--row` says how far an equalize reaches and means nothing beside a direction, so it is refused rather than quietly ignored: a caller that typed it wanted the panes beside this one evened out, and a resize that dropped it would move one divider and report success. Refused against the four directions rather than made to require `--equalize`, because a bool flag is present in clap's sense whether or not it was typed - so a requirement on one is a requirement nothing can fail.

cases.name: the keyboard steps to the next pane
cases.why: The chord's other door. `next` and `previous` walk reading order across every region and wrap, so between them they reach every pane the window is showing - which is the guarantee the four directions do not make.

cases.name: the keyboard steps geometrically
cases.why: The four directions are about where a pane is on screen rather than where it sits in a list, and they do not wrap. Spelled with the same four words a split uses, so a caller that reads a side out of an answer can send it straight back.

cases.name: a pane is reached by the number drawn beside it
cases.why: `muster window` prints a place for every pane and nothing consumed it until now, which left a number a script could read and not act on. This is cmd+3 from a script.

cases.name: the pane that asked is reached without knowing which it is
cases.why: The chord that goes to the most urgent pane asking for somebody, from a script. It names no pane because finding one is the point: the window knows which pane has waited longest, and a caller would have to reconstruct that from `muster window` and would get the order wrong.

cases.name: a group's transcript is opened from a script as its banner opens it
cases.why: Choosing a message's banner, or the chord that goes to what asks, opens the group's transcript, and a command line has to reach the same place (MIP-4, section 10). It is the one msg verb sent to the window rather than the daemon, since a transcript is a pane. It names no daemon: the one on this machine keeps messages for the human, a group kept elsewhere included under its full name.

cases.name: going back is the mouse's back button from a script
cases.why: The focus history lives in the window, so a script walks the same one the mouse buttons and cmd+opt+[ do rather than keeping its own. It names no pane because the window is the only thing that knows where the keyboard has been.

cases.name: going forward again is the same request the other way
cases.why: One request with a direction rather than two, because back and forward are one history walked two ways, and the window answers both with where it went.

cases.name: a step back and a pane are two answers to one question
cases.why: Going back names its own destination, so a pane beside it is a caller who has not decided where the keyboard goes.

cases.name: a pane and a direction are two answers to one question
cases.why: Where to put the keyboard has one answer. A name, a direction and a place are three ways of giving it, and two at once is a caller who has not decided.

cases.name: the config file is read again on request
cases.why: The fourth door onto one action: a chord, a menu item, a saved file and this all arrive at the same reload. Worth having from a script because editing the file and applying it are two acts, and a script that writes one wants to finish the job.

cases.name: the agent list is shown or put away
cases.why: A toggle rather than a set, matching what the chord and the menu item send: neither of them knows which way the list currently is, and the window does.

cases.name: text is made bigger in the pane the keyboard is on
cases.why: The window's own three words rather than English ones like `bigger`, on the rule the four sides follow. No pane is named because none can be: the request carries no pane id, and what it means is the pane in front of whoever asked.

cases.name: a font change nobody has is refused
cases.why: Three changes exist and clap knows all three, so a fourth is caught out here with the list beside it rather than by the window with a request already sent.

cases.name: a pane is read back
cases.why: The half of a pane an agent could not see. `muster window` says what state every agent is in and what it claims to be doing, and neither of those is what the pane printed - so an agent watching another one could tell that it had stopped and not why.

cases.name: a read with no rows asks for as much as there is
cases.why: Zero is what the window reads as `as far as you will go`, and it is also what an absent number sends - so a caller with nothing particular in mind and a caller who said nothing make the same request rather than two that have to be kept in agreement.

cases.name: a read can ask for the last few rows only
cases.why: An agent checking whether a command finished wants the bottom of the pane, not a thousand rows of it. Said as a count rather than left to the caller to trim, so the rows never cross the wire.

cases.name: windows are listed without naming one
cases.why: The one read that cannot be narrowed to a window: the question is which windows there are. Every window of an app answers on one socket, so this asks every app under this home - one, unless two installs are running - and lists each window it describes.

expect.answers_here: listing every open window under this home

cases.name: a command names its window with --window
cases.why: Every window of an app answers on one socket, so outside every pane a command that names nothing reaches the window in front. `--window` names the one meant, on any command, as the request's window rather than in its payload (mip/0006-one-process.md, Open Questions).

cases.name: for a tab move, --window is where the tab goes
cases.why: The window a move is about is the one the tab goes to, so `--window` fills the move's destination and the request names no window of its own - the same request `tab move --window` has always sent.

cases.name: --window on a command about every window is refused
cases.why: A flag that silently does nothing is one nobody finds out did nothing. Listing windows, opening one and reopening one are not about a window that is open.

expect.refused: --window window-2 names the window a command is about, and this command is not about one window, so nothing was done. `muster window reopen window-2` brings a closed window back.

cases.name: closed windows are listed on their own
cases.why: A window somebody closed stays closed, keeps its tabs, and comes back by name with `muster window reopen NAME` (mip/0006-one-process.md, section 4). This is where the name is found.

expect.answers_here: listing every closed window under this home

cases.name: making a window asks the running app for it
cases.why: Every window of an install is a window of one process (mip/0006-one-process.md), so a new window is asked of the app that is running, which opens it beside the windows it has. Only when none answers does the command start the app. It is the only verb here that is not something the keyboard could send instead, because the case it has to cover is having no app to ask.

expect.answers_here: asking the running app for a window

cases.name: a window can be asked for with its first tab on one machine
cases.why: A window asked for takes its first tab on the first machine here, and with a devenv attached that may be the wrong one. `pane new` and `tab new` already take --daemon with this meaning.

expect.answers_here: asking the running app for a window with its first tab on devenv

cases.name: a window can be asked for onto a tab that already exists
cases.why: The only other way to put an existing tab in a window of its own was a new window and then `tab move`, which leaves a tab nobody wanted behind it. The tab moves into the window, from whichever window held it.

expect.answers_here: asking the running app for a window onto t1w3r07bsd

cases.name: a machine and a tab together are refused
cases.why: A window opened onto a tab has its first tab already, so a machine to ask for one says nothing, and taking it silently would leave a caller thinking it had.

cases.name: closing a window asks the running app to close it
cases.why: A window closed only from the GUI could not be closed by an agent or covered by a script. The app closes it as its close button would, so the window keeps its tabs for `muster window reopen`. With no name it is the window this command is about, as for any command.

expect.answers_here: asking the running app to close the window this is about

cases.name: a window to close can be named either way
cases.why: `--window` names the window any command is about, so it names the one to close as the argument does. The same name twice is one window.

expect.answers_here: asking the running app to close window-2

cases.name: two windows named to close are refused
cases.why: Either name could be the one meant, and closing the wrong window is not something to guess at.

expect.refused: `muster window close window-2` and --window window-3 name two windows, so nothing was closed. Name one.

cases.name: a bare window read is still a read
cases.why: `muster window` kept its meaning when `window` grew subcommands under it. A caller that had this in a script before is asking the same thing after, which is the whole reason the subcommand is optional.

cases.name: a window that was closed is brought back
cases.why: The gap this closes: New Window made a fresh one and nothing reopened the last, so the only way back to a window you had closed was to rebuild it by hand. Asked of the running app, as `window new` is, and the two differ only in which arrangement the window opens onto - the window closed last, which comes back onto the tabs it kept.

expect.answers_here: asking the running app for the window closed last

cases.name: a closed window is brought back by name
cases.why: A window somebody closed stays closed, and the one closed last is not always the one wanted back: `muster window` lists closed windows under their names, and this takes one of those names (mip/0006-one-process.md, section 4).

expect.answers_here: asking the running app for window-3
